_comment: Where a fact comes from, and exactly when it became public. The same shape as sources.json and for a stricter reason: a price that arrives late is a missing price, but a news item that arrives EARLY is invented skill. Every item carries published_utc from the provider's own record, and an advisor is only ever shown items whose published_utc is strictly before the moment it was asked. Anything without a publication instant is collected and never shown. All three families are public domain and redistributable, which is why they were chosen over a commercial wire.

families.stamp_note: EDGAR's acceptance instant is when the filing became publicly retrievable. A company's own press release often precedes it, so this stamp is late rather than early relative to what the market knew — the safe direction. Showing an item sooner than this would be inventing knowledge; showing it later only weakens a real effect.

The keyless CSV gives observations, not release instants: the August CPI figure is published in mid-September, and treating the observation date as the publication date would hand every advisor a month of hindsight. So these items are recorded with published_utc null and are NEVER shown. They are still collected daily because FRED revises its history — what a series said on a given day cannot be recovered from FRED later without the vintage API.
families.licence: public domain (US government work), per series

series.what: US consumer price index, all items, seasonally adjusted

families.stamp_note: A schedule is not news. That the committee meets on a given date has been public for a year, so a calendar entry may be shown before the date without any hindsight at all — what happens at the meeting is a separate fact that this family does not carry. Recorded verbatim from the Federal Reserve's own calendar page, fetched 2026-09-04; the page states every date is tentative until confirmed at the meeting immediately preceding it, and it publishes no release times, so none are stored here.
